summary: This unit teaches you to keep a fabrication workshop clean, orderly and safe, and at Level 3 to plan, lead and check the housekeeping for a bay, a job or a team. You will learn to spot the hazards that poor housekeeping causes, use the 5S method, clean safely, handle chemicals with their safety data sheets, deal with spills, store materials, tools and gas cylinders correctly, separate and dispose of waste, inspect and score the workshop, and coach others to keep to the standard.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). **Housekeeping** is the everyday work of keeping the workplace clean, tidy, organised and safe: clearing slag, stubs and offcuts, storing materials and tools, controlling spills and waste, and keeping exits and fire equipment clear.

At Level 2 you kept your own bench and booth in order. At Level 3 you **plan and lead** housekeeping: you decide what must be done and how often, share the tasks fairly, make sure the right equipment is there, inspect and score the area, record what you find, see that faults are put right, and set the example for the team.

Good housekeeping is not about looks. Many of the trips, falls, fires and lost hours in a fabrication shop start with clutter: a lead across a walkway, a pile of card near a grinding bench, an oil leak nobody reported, a tool that is never where it should be.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 welders and fabricators, team leaders, and anyone who looks after a workshop, a store or a site compound.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Plan housekeeping
List the tasks for a bay or job, set how often each is done, give each one an owner on a roster, and allow the time in the job plan.
Spot and control hazards
Trips, slips, fire, falling stock, blocked exits, damaged leads and torn screens: find them and deal with them.
Use the 5S method
Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise and Sustain, with red tags, marked places and a written standard.
Clean safely
Use the right method for dust, swarf, slag and spills; isolate machines before cleaning; look after the fume extraction.
Handle chemicals and spills
Read the label and safety data sheet, store and dilute products correctly, and lead a spill response.
Store materials, tools and cylinders
Keep racks within their ratings, give every tool a place, and store gas cylinders upright, secured and apart.
Separate and dispose of waste
Scrap metal, general waste and hazardous waste in the right bins, collected by the right people, never into drains or a fire.
Inspect, record and report
Use a checklist, score the area, give every fault an owner and a date, report near misses, and keep the records.
Lead others
Brief the team, coach people who fall short, check the standard every day, and follow up.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, hazards, fire and emergency access, inspections, cleaning methods, machines, chemicals, waste, gas cylinders, storage, extraction, 5S and supervising others.

A **written paper** with short answers (5S steps, spill kit, red tag, wet floor sign, a dilution sum, an inspection percentage, shadow board, fire watch, NEPA, lux, chocks) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Two group practicals:** a 5S improvement of a fabrication bay with before and after scores; and a workshop inspection with a spill drill and a waste segregation station.

blocks.note: The assessor watches how you work, not only what the bay looks like at the end: isolating equipment before cleaning it, wearing the right PPE, using safe cleaning methods, and putting each kind of waste in the right bin.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Housekeeping is part of every job, not something left for Friday afternoon. Slag, stubs, offcuts and spills build up within hours, and every hour they stay they make trips, fires and lost time more likely. A Level 3 welder plans it in, like any other task.

flow: List every housekeeping task for the bay or job
Decide how often each one is done: as you go, at the end of each shift, weekly, or as the maker's manual says
Give each task to a named person on a roster, sharing the work fairly
Allow the time in the job plan, so cleaning is done as the work goes and not skipped when the job runs late
Make sure the brooms, vacuum, bins, spill kit, signs and PPE are there and working
Explain the plan and the reasons at a toolbox talk
Check every day, inspect every week with the checklist, record the score and act on the faults

blocks.p: For a big job that will make a lot of offcuts and packing over several days, put marked scrap bins beside the job and empty them every day, agree a laydown area for incoming steel, and keep the marked walkways clear the whole time.

ul: **Set the example.** A team copies its leader. If your own leads lie across the walkway, nobody else will coil theirs.
**Brief clearly.** Explain what is to be done, by whom, and why it matters: trips, fire, lost tools, and how the shop looks to customers.
**Share fairly.** Rotate the unpleasant jobs. Giving all the sweeping to the newest trainee is unfair and teaches nobody else anything.
**Check and give feedback.** Look at each area at the end of the shift. Praise what is done well; point out what was missed, calmly and at once.

blocks.h: Coaching someone who does not keep the standard

flow: Talk to the person in private and ask why
Explain the reasons with real examples: a trip on a lead, a fire started in a pile of card, an hour lost looking for a tool
Show the standard: what a finished bay looks like, where each tool lives, which waste goes in which bin
Work alongside them the first time, then agree clear tasks on the roster
Check their area each shift and give fair, specific feedback
If nothing changes, talk again, record it, and refer it to the supervisor

blocks.note: Picking up after someone "to keep the peace" fixes nothing: the problem comes back tomorrow, and the rest of the team learns that the standard does not matter.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Painted lines mark the **walkways** that must stay clear of work, stock and bins, so that people, trolleys and forklifts can move safely and everyone can reach the exits. Colours differ between workplaces: many use yellow or white for walkways, red for areas around fire equipment, and yellow-and-black stripes for hazards. Learn your Centre's colours, and never let work spread across a line.

ul: Exits, escape routes and fire doors are never blocked, wedged open or locked while people are inside.
Fire extinguishers hang on their brackets, near exits, where they can be seen and reached: not behind stock, not locked away, and not under a bench where spatter falls on them.

Check each extinguisher's gauge and seal on your inspection. A gauge needle out of the green zone, a broken seal or a missing pin means it may not work: replace it with a working one and report it for servicing.
Clean up oil and fuel spills before any welding, cutting or grinding in that area.

After hot work, keep the fire watch for the time the hot-work permit or the Centre's rules give, often 30 to 60 minutes, and check hidden places such as cracks in floors and walls. Do not end it while there is any smoke or smell of burning.

blocks.p: Good light lets people see hazards and do accurate work. The light falling on a surface is measured in **lux** with a light meter. Workshop guides often suggest around 300 lux for general welding and fitting, and 500 lux or more for fine work such as marking out and inspection; stores and corridors need less. Report failed lights at once, and arrange temporary lighting if accurate work must go on.

blocks.note: Many Jamaican workshops have open sides. Afternoon showers blow in and wet the floor near the openings, so keep leads off the floor there and mop up quickly. Water standing in old drums, tyres, buckets and offcut piles in the yard is where mosquitoes breed, including the kind that spreads dengue: tip it out, cover what must stay outside, and keep the yard clear.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **5S** is a method, first used in Japanese factories, for organising a workplace so that it stays safe, clean and efficient. Each of the five steps begins with S, in English and in the Japanese words.

head: Step
What it means
Fabrication workshop example
rows: 1 Sort (seiri)
Remove everything that is not needed for the work. Put a red tag on anything doubtful.
Broken clamps, worn-out discs, empty tins, old offcuts and jigs nobody uses are tagged and moved out.
2 Set in order (seiton)
Give every needed item a set, marked place, close to where it is used.
A shadow board for hand tools; labelled racks for bar by size; a painted bay for the cylinder trolley; the electrode oven beside the booths.
3 Shine (seiso)
Clean the area and the equipment, and look for faults while you clean.
Sweeping the booths and wiping down isolated machines, and noticing a leaking hose or a cracked screen.
4 Standardise (seiketsu)
Write down how the area should look and how it is kept, so everyone works the same way.
A photo of the finished bay, a one-page standard, a checklist and a cleaning roster posted in the bay.
5 Sustain (shitsuke)
Keep it up as a habit, with training, regular audits and leaders setting the example.
A quick daily check, a weekly score posted on the board, and new trainees shown the standard on their first day.

blocks.h: Red tags and the holding area

ul: During Sort, any item whose use is in doubt gets a **red tag** with the date, who tagged it, why, and where it came from.
Tagged items go to a marked **holding area**, not straight into the skip.
After a set time, often one or two weeks, the supervisor decides: keep it and give it a marked place, move it to another area that needs it, sell it, or dispose of it properly.
Never throw away an item that might belong to a client or another job without asking.

blocks.h: Running a 5S improvement of a bay

flow: Take 'before' photos from a fixed spot and score the bay with the housekeeping checklist
Write a short plan: the tasks, who leads each step, the PPE and the time for each
Sort: red-tag and remove what is not needed
Set in order: mark a place for every item that stays
Shine: clean the bay, bench and equipment, with the equipment switched off and isolated
Standardise: write a one-page standard and a roster, and post them in the bay
Sustain: score the bay again, take 'after' photos from the same spot, and agree how it will be checked from now on

blocks.p: Showing the improvement as a score makes it real. If the bay scored 22 out of 40 checklist items before (22 ÷ 40 × 100 = 55%) and 35 out of 40 after (87.5%), the score rose by 32.5 percentage points.

blocks.note: Most 5S projects fail at the last step. A bay that is spotless on Friday is back to its old state within weeks unless someone checks it every day and scores it every week, and the leaders keep to the standard themselves.
blocks.label: Remember

Bare hands; plastic or paper bins

With the machine stopped and isolated: a swarf hook, brush or magnetic pick-up, wearing gloves

blocks.note: Never use compressed air to clean your clothes, hair or skin. It drives dust and metal into eyes and skin, and air forced into a cut can be very dangerous. Use a brush or a vacuum.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Stop the machine
Switch off and isolate it: unplug it, or switch off and lock the isolator with your own lock and a tag
Wait until every moving part has stopped and hot parts have cooled
Put on gloves and eye protection
Remove swarf with a brush or swarf hook, never with your fingers
Clean as the maker's manual says, looking for damage, leaks and loose guards
Refit the guards, remove your lock and tag, and check the machine before handing it back

blocks.p: Your own lock and tag on the isolator mean that nobody can switch the machine on while your hands are in it. A note on the switch, or a friend asked to "keep an eye on it", is not enough.

blocks.h: End-of-shift clean-down of a welding bay

flow: Finish the run; drop the stub in the metal bin; hang up the holder or gun
Switch off and isolate the welding set; close the cylinder valves and bleed the hoses as the maker's instructions say
Leave hot work to cool in a safe place, marked HOT
Chip and sweep slag and spatter into the metal bin; offcuts into the scrap bin
Vacuum or damp-wipe grinding dust from the bench and floor
Coil leads and hoses and hang them up, checking them for damage as you go
Put tools back on the shadow board
Check the bay for smouldering, then report any faults

ul: Clogged filters cut the airflow, so less fume is drawn away from the welder's face. The welder may not notice until they feel ill.
Empty the **spark trap** or pre-filter regularly: hot sparks reaching a dirty filter can start a fire inside the unit.

Clean or change the filters only as the maker's manual says, with the unit switched off. Wear gloves and the respirator the manual or the instructor gives, bag the old filter and dispose of it as the manual says.
Record each filter change, and check that the hood or arm is placed close to the arc when the bay is set up again.

blocks.p: Check screens and curtains as part of the clean-down. A tear or gap lets arc light out, where it can burn the eyes of people walking past. Report damaged screens and have them repaired or replaced before the bay is used again.

sections.title: Chemicals, safety data sheets and spills

blocks.p: Every degreaser, solvent, paint, thinner, anti-spatter spray and penetrant comes with a **label** and a **safety data sheet (SDS)** from the maker. The SDS has 16 numbered sections. Read it before anyone uses a new product, and keep the SDS file where everyone can reach it.

head: SDS section
What it tells you
rows: 2 Hazards
What the product can do to people and the environment, with the warning pictograms
4 First aid
What to do if it is swallowed, breathed in, or gets on the skin or in the eyes
5 Firefighting
Which extinguishers to use, and the dangers in a fire
6 Accidental release
How to deal with a spill: PPE, containment and clean-up
7 Handling and storage
How to use and store it safely, and what to keep it away from
8 Exposure controls and PPE
Ventilation, gloves, eye and breathing protection
13 Disposal
How to dispose of the product, its waste and empty containers

ul: Choose the least harmful product that will do the job, such as a water-based degreaser instead of a strong solvent.
Use it with good ventilation, away from welding, cutting, grinding and any other source of ignition.
Wear the gloves, eye protection and other PPE the SDS asks for.
Never put a chemical into a drinks bottle or any unmarked container. Label every container you fill, with the product name and its hazard.
**Never mix products.** Bleach mixed with ammonia cleaners gives off toxic gases; bleach mixed with acid descalers gives off chlorine.
Keep chlorinated degreasers away from welding: arc light can turn their vapour into a poisonous gas.
Wash your hands after use and before eating or smoking.

blocks.p: "1 part to 15 parts water" means 16 parts in total. To make 8 litres: 8 000 mL ÷ 16 = 500 mL of concentrate, made up with 7.5 litres of water. Dilute only as the label says: a stronger mix wastes product and may harm skin or surfaces; a weaker one does not clean.

blocks.note: Some labels write "1 in 20", meaning 1 part in 20 parts of finished solution, and others "1 to 20", meaning 1 part to 20 parts of water. Read the label carefully and ask if you are not sure.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Keep every container closed and labelled.
Store flammable liquids such as thinners, solvents and paints in a fire-safe (flammables) cabinet or store, ventilated, out of the sun and away from heat, hot work and oxygen cylinders.
Keep only the day's amount at the bench, in a labelled safety container.
Keep products apart that the SDS says must not be stored together.
Keep a spill kit near the chemical store.

flow: Warn people and keep them away; put out wet floor signs or barriers
If it is safe, stop the source: switch off and isolate a leaking machine, stand a fallen tin upright, put a drip tray under the leak
If you do not know what the liquid is, check the SDS; put on gloves, boots and eye protection
Contain it: lay absorbent socks around the edge, starting on the side towards any drain or doorway
Absorb it: cover the spill with pads or granules from the spill kit
Bag the used absorbent, label it and put it with the hazardous waste, not in the general bin
Clean the floor with a suitable degreaser and check it is dry before the signs come down
Allow no welding, cutting or grinding nearby until the area is clean
Report the spill and the leak, tag the machine out of use until it is repaired, and refill the spill kit

blocks.note: Floor drains in many workshops run straight to a gully, soakaway or river, not to a treatment plant. Oil and solvent washed into them pollute water and land, and the law forbids it. The National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) deals with pollution of the environment.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Storing materials, tools and gas cylinders

head: Item
How to store it
Why
rows: Long bar, pipe and sections
Flat on racks, sorted by size and grade, labelled
No ends sticking out into walkways
Round bar and pipe held with chocks so they cannot roll
No trips or rolling stock; easy to find
Sheet and plate
In a sheet rack, or flat on bearers
Within the rack's marked load rating
Never leaned loosely against a wall or rack
A sliding sheet can crush feet and legs
Heavy items on shelving
On the lowest shelves; light items higher up
Safer to lift, and less likely to fall
Offcuts
On an offcut rack, sorted and marked with size and grade
They can be found and used again
Hand tools
On a shadow board (painted outline of each tool) or in labelled drawers
A missing tool is seen at once and can be traced
Power tools
Dry, on a shelf, with leads loosely coiled
Protects the leads and the tool
Welding consumables
Dry, in sealed packs; opened low-hydrogen electrodes in the holding oven
Damp flux causes porosity and cracking
Gas cylinders
Upright, secured, capped, in a ventilated, shaded store, oxygen apart from fuel gases, full apart from empty
Prevents falls, leaks, fires and mix-ups

blocks.p: Every rack has a **safe working load** for each level or arm, marked by the maker. Work out the load before you stack. A plate 2.0 m × 1.0 m × 8 mm thick has a volume of 2.0 × 1.0 × 0.008 = 0.016 m³ and a mass of 0.016 × 7850 = 125.6 kg. On a level rated 1 000 kg, 7 plates (879 kg) are within the rating; 8 plates (1 005 kg) are over it.

ul: Never climb racks or shelving.
Report racks that are bent, leaning, damaged by a forklift or missing their locking pins, and keep them empty until checked.
Load from the bottom up, heaviest first, and unload from the top down.
Keep cylinders **upright** and secured with a chain, strap or bracket, in the store and on the trolley.
Fit the valve cap whenever the cylinder is not connected.
Store them in a ventilated, shaded, dry place, away from heat, hot work, oil and grease.
Keep oxygen apart from fuel gases such as acetylene and LPG, by the distance or fire-resistant wall your Centre's rules give.
Keep full and empty cylinders apart. Mark empties EMPTY so nobody connects one by mistake, and return them to the supplier.
Acetylene must always stand upright. If you find one lying down, stand it up, secure it, and leave it for the time the supplier gives before it is used.
Move cylinders on a trolley, never by rolling them on their sides or lifting them by the valve.

blocks.note: Never let oil or grease touch an oxygen valve, regulator or fitting, and never wipe one with an oily rag or handle it with greasy gloves. Oil and grease can ignite violently in contact with high-pressure oxygen.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Waste segregation** means keeping different kinds of waste apart, in labelled bins, so that each can be recycled or disposed of in the right way. Mixed waste is harder and dearer to deal with, and hazardous waste mixed with general waste ends up in the wrong place.

head: Waste
Where it goes
Points to know
rows: Clean steel offcuts, swarf, electrode stubs
Scrap metal bin, then a licensed scrap metal dealer for recycling
Keep stainless steel and aluminium in their own bins: sorted scrap is worth more
Paper, card, packing, food waste
General waste bin, collected by the waste collection service
Keep it away from hot work
Oily, paint- or solvent-soaked rags
A metal bin with a self-closing lid, emptied daily to the hazardous waste store
Some oils, oil-based paints and stains can heat up and catch fire by themselves; the lid starves a fire of air
Used oil, solvents, paint waste, used absorbent
Closed, labelled containers in the hazardous waste store, collected by an approved collector
Never into drains, onto the ground or into a fire
Empty gas cylinders
Marked EMPTY, stored apart, returned to the supplier
Never scrapped or cut up
Fluorescent tubes, batteries
Kept whole, stored apart, sent to an approved collector
Tubes contain mercury; batteries contain lead, acid or other harmful metals
Cracked or worn grinding discs
Taken out of use and binned so nobody can pick them up again
A cracked disc can burst at speed
Empty paint and chemical tins
As the SDS says; treat as hazardous unless clean and dry
Some still hold flammable vapour

ul: Labelled bins with a sign showing what goes in each, using pictures as well as words.
A scrap metal bin, a general waste bin, a closed metal bin for oily rags, and a container for hazardous waste.
Close to where the waste is made, but clear of walkways and exits.
Emptied on a schedule written on the roster.
Records kept of each collection of hazardous waste and scrap: who collected it, how much, and the receipt or transfer note.

blocks.note: Do not burn rubbish in a drum or on the ground. Smoke from paint, plastic, rubber and oily rags is toxic, it upsets neighbours, and in the dry months a fire in the yard can spread into bush and grass. Pollution of land, air and water is a matter for NEPA, and waste collection is organised through the National Solid Waste Management Authority (NSWMA) and licensed haulers.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A housekeeping inspection uses a written **checklist**, so that every area is checked the same way each time and nothing is forgotten. A good checklist covers: walkways and exits; floors and spills; benches and booths; racks and shelving; gas cylinders; cables, leads and hoses; tools; chemicals; waste bins; fire extinguishers and alarms; lighting; fume extraction; welding screens; and the first-aid box.

flow: Agree the time with the supervisor and collect the checklist, a pen and a camera
Walk the whole area in a set order, looking closely, including behind racks and under benches
Mark each item satisfactory or not; for each fault, write what it is, where, and how serious
Deal with dangerous faults at once: stop the use, tag the item out of use and report it
Put every other fault on an action list with an owner and a date
Work out the score as a percentage, to compare with the last inspection
Sign and date the checklist, give a copy to the supervisor, and check later that each action was done

blocks.p: **Working out the score:** if 43 of 50 items are satisfactory, the score is 43 ÷ 50 × 100 = 86%.

blocks.label: Remember

head: What
Example

A split lead, a cracked screen, a leaking hose
Take it out of use, fix an out-of-service (DO NOT USE) tag with the date, the fault and your name, and report it

blocks.p: Keep the signed checklists, action lists, rosters, filter-change records and waste collection receipts on file. They show what was checked and that the faults were fixed; they reveal problems that keep coming back; and they are the evidence an auditor, an inspector or an investigation will ask for.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can plan the housekeeping for a bay or job: the tasks, how often, who does each, and the time in the job plan.
I can lead and coach a team to keep the standard, and follow up when someone does not.
I can name the hazards that poor housekeeping causes and the control for each.
I can keep walkways, exits and fire equipment clear, and check extinguishers on an inspection.
I can explain the five steps of 5S with a workshop example of each, and use red tags and a holding area.
I can run a 5S improvement and show it with before and after scores.
I can choose a safe cleaning method for dust, slag, swarf and spills, and explain why compressed air and dry sweeping are not used.
I can isolate and lock off a machine before cleaning it, and clean down a welding bay at the end of a shift.
I can look after fume extraction filters and spark traps as the maker says.
I can find what I need on a safety data sheet, dilute a concentrate correctly, and store chemicals safely.
I can lead a spill response from warning people to refilling the spill kit.
I can store bar, plate, tools and consumables correctly and keep racks within their load ratings.
I can store and handle gas cylinders safely and keep oil away from oxygen fittings.
I can separate waste into the right bins and say how each kind is disposed of.
I can carry out an inspection, score it, write an action list with owners and dates, and keep the records.
I can report faulty equipment, near misses and accidents correctly.

terms: 5S
A method for organising a workplace: Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain
Action list
A list of faults found, each with an action, an owner and a date
Chock
A wedge placed against round bar or pipe so it cannot roll
Fire watch
A person who watches for fire during hot work and for a set time after it
Holding area
A marked place where red-tagged items wait for a decision
Housekeeping
Keeping the workplace clean, tidy, organised and safe
Isolation
Cutting a machine off from its power source, and locking it off, before work on it
Load rating
The safe working load a rack, shelf or arm is made to carry
Lux
The unit of light falling on a surface
Near miss
An event that could have hurt someone but did not
NEPA
The National Environment and Planning Agency, which deals with pollution of the environment
Out-of-service tag
A tag fixed to faulty equipment so nobody uses it until it is repaired
Red tag
A tag on an item that may not be needed, so a decision can be made about it
Roster
A list that gives each task to a named person, with how often it is done
SDS
Safety data sheet: the maker's 16-section sheet on a product's hazards and safe use
Segregation
Keeping different kinds of waste apart in separate bins
Set in order
The 5S step that gives every needed item a set, marked place
Shadow board
A board with painted tool outlines, showing where each tool is kept
Shine
The 5S step of cleaning the area and equipment and looking for faults while cleaning
Sort
The 5S step of removing items that are not needed
Spark trap
The part of a fume extractor that catches sparks before they reach the filter
Spill kit
A kit of absorbent socks, pads, granules and bags kept ready for spills
Standardise
The 5S step of writing down the standard so everyone works the same way
Sustain
The 5S step of keeping the good habits going over time
Swarf
Metal chips and curls made by drilling, sawing and machining
Walkway
A marked route that must be kept clear for people and trolleys
Wet floor sign
A sign warning that a floor is wet or has a spill

c1.title: A shared bay for hotel stairs in Ocho Rios
c1.text: Kemoy Lindo is the Level 3 team leader in Bay 2 of a fabrication shop in Ocho Rios, St Ann, where two shifts are building steel stairs for a hotel. His first roster gave all the end-of-shift cleaning to Shavar, the newest trainee. The team then ran a 5S clean-up of the bay: on the housekeeping checklist it scored 22 of 40 items satisfactory before and 35 of 40 after, and the team pinned up a photo of the finished bay beside a new cleaning roster. Three weeks later the bay has slipped back to its old state.

c2.title: A coolant leak in Hayes
c2.text: Tanisha Brown leads the morning crew at a fabrication shop in Hayes, Clarendon. The pump on the band saw has leaked a pool of coolant that is spreading across the floor towards a floor drain by the door. The spill kit hangs by the store. The shop's floor degreaser is a concentrate mixed 1 part to 15 parts water, and Tanisha will need 8 litres of solution to clean the floor afterwards.

c3.title: The store yard in Lucea
c3.text: Jermaine Gayle runs the store at a steel shop in Lucea, Hanover. A new delivery of 8 mm plate, cut to 2.0 m × 1.0 m, is to go on a rack level marked "SWL 1 000 kg". In the gas cage, a fitter has just wiped a sticky oxygen regulator with an oily rag. After a week of heavy rain, water is standing in an old drum and among a pile of offcuts behind the store.

c4.title: Hot work in a hardware warehouse in Port Maria
c4.text: Oneil Francis is welding new shelf brackets inside the timber-walled warehouse of a hardware store in Port Maria, St Mary. The hot-work permit asks for a fire watch for 30 minutes after welding stops. During the pre-work check, Oneil finds that the needle on the nearest extinguisher's gauge is in the red zone. When the job is finished, a trainee suggests burning the cardboard packing and the oily rags in a drum behind the building.

c5.title: Closing the shop in Golden Grove
c5.text: Davian, a Level 3 trainee, is closing a small fabrication shop in Golden Grove, St Thomas, for the night. He sees a trainee blowing metal dust off his overalls with the compressed air line. The guillotine needs swarf and offcuts cleared from around the blade. Two fluorescent tubes over the marking-out bench failed during the afternoon, and trainees there made several marking mistakes. The fume extractor in the welding bay has not been checked this week.

questions.q: What was wrong with Kemoy's first roster?
o: All tasks fell on one person; they should be shared
Nothing: the newest trainee should always do the cleaning
It should have left cleaning to the end of the week
It should have given the cleaning to the shop's cleaner
questions.why: A roster shares tasks fairly and names an owner for each, so the work gets done in every booth and everyone keeps the standard. Loading it onto the newest person is unfair, and the others learn that cleaning is not their job.

questions.q: By how many percentage points did the bay's checklist score rise?
o: 32.5 points
13 points
37.1 points
59 points
questions.why: Before: 22 ÷ 40 × 100 = 55%. After: 35 ÷ 40 × 100 = 87.5%. The rise is 87.5 − 55 = 32.5 percentage points. Counting items (35 − 22 = 13) does not give a percentage.

questions.q: Pinning up a photo of the finished bay beside a cleaning roster is which step of 5S?
o: Sort
Shine
Set in order
Standardise
questions.why: Standardise means writing down, or showing, how the area should look and how it is kept, so that everyone works the same way. Photos, a one-page standard, checklists and rosters are its tools.

questions.q: Three weeks later the bay is back to its old state. Which step was weak, and what fixes it?
o: Sort: throw out even more of the tools and equipment
Sustain: check it daily and score it every week
Shine: hire a cleaner to do the whole bay each evening
Set in order: paint new outlines on the shadow board
questions.why: Sustain is keeping the habit going. Without someone checking every day, scoring every week and setting the example, a bay slips back within weeks, however good the clean-up was.

questions.q: Where should Tanisha's team lay the absorbent socks?
o: Across the middle of the pool, to split it in two
Only around the saw, where the leak started
Round the edge, beginning on the drain side
In the drain itself, to soak up what runs in
questions.why: Containment comes before absorbing: the socks stop the spill spreading, and the first priority is to keep it out of the drain, which may run straight to a gully or river. Pads or granules then soak up the pool.

questions.q: How much degreaser concentrate is needed for the 8 litres of solution?
o: 533 mL
500 mL
1.2 litres
800 mL
questions.why: 1 part to 15 parts water makes 16 parts in all, so 8 000 mL ÷ 16 = 500 mL of concentrate with 7.5 litres of water. Dividing by 15 forgets the concentrate's own part.

questions.q: What should happen to the used absorbent pads and socks?
o: Put in the general bin, as the coolant is now soaked up
Rinsed out in the sink and kept for the next spill
Left to dry in the sun, then thrown in the skip
Bagged, labelled and kept with the hazardous waste
questions.why: Absorbent full of coolant or oil is hazardous waste. It is bagged and labelled, stored with the hazardous waste and collected by an approved collector. Rinsing it washes the coolant into the drains anyway.

questions.q: What should be done about the band saw?
o: Wipe it down and carry on cutting while the pump still works
Isolate it, tag it out of use and report the faulty pump
Turn the coolant off and cut dry until the pump is replaced
Put a drip tray under it and leave it running for now
questions.why: The leak is the cause of the spill, and a saw run dry or left leaking will cause more trouble. Isolating and tagging it stops anyone using it until the pump is repaired, and the report gets the repair done.

questions.q: How many of the plates may go on the rack level?
o: 8 plates
10 plates
7 plates
6 plates
questions.why: Each plate is 2.0 × 1.0 × 0.008 = 0.016 m³; × 7850 kg/m³ = 125.6 kg. Seven plates are 879 kg, inside the 1 000 kg rating; eight would be about 1 005 kg, over it.

questions.q: Why is it dangerous to wipe the oxygen regulator with an oily rag?
o: The oil will make the regulator gauge read too high
Oil can ignite violently in high-pressure oxygen
Oil makes the threads too slippery for the fitting to hold
The rag's fibres will block the oxygen hose
questions.why: Oil and grease can catch fire violently, without a spark, when high-pressure oxygen reaches them. Oxygen fittings are kept clean and dry, and handled with clean hands and gloves.

questions.q: Why should the water standing behind the store be dealt with as part of housekeeping?
o: The water will make the offcuts too heavy to lift
Standing water rots the timber bearers under the racks
It is only a problem if a visitor sees it
Mosquitoes that spread dengue breed in it
questions.why: Mosquitoes that spread dengue breed in small pools of standing water, such as in drums, tyres and junk piles. Tipping out the water and clearing the yard removes their breeding places.

questions.q: At 25 minutes into the fire watch, the watcher smells smoke and sees a wisp coming from a crack in the timber wall. What should happen?
o: End the watch at 30 minutes, as the permit says
Note it on the permit and check again in the morning
Spray water on the wall, then end the watch at once
Find and put out the source, then restart the watch
questions.why: The permit's time is a minimum. Smoke means something is smouldering: it is found and put out (raise the alarm and call 110 if it cannot be reached or controlled at once), the area is checked again, and the watch starts again from then and goes on until there is no sign of fire. Then it is reported.

questions.q: What should Oneil do about the extinguisher with its gauge needle in the red?
o: Use it anyway, as it may still work for a small fire
Shake it well to move the needle back into the green
Replace it before welding and report it for service
Leave it on its bracket and keep a bucket of water nearby
questions.why: A needle out of the green means the extinguisher may not work. A working extinguisher must be in place before hot work starts, and the faulty one is reported so it is serviced or replaced.

questions.q: Why should the packing and oily rags not be burned in a drum?
o: The smoke is toxic and the fire can spread
Burning is fine for card but not for rags
Burning is fine as long as it is after dark
The drum will rust through after a few fires
questions.why: Burning oily rags, paint and plastic gives off toxic smoke and pollutes the air, and a yard fire can spread to buildings or bush. Card goes in the general waste and rags in the hazardous waste for an approved collector.

questions.q: What should Davian say to the trainee using the air line on his overalls?
o: Turn the pressure down so the air does not tear the cloth
Stop, as it drives dust into eyes and skin
Only blow the overalls when no one else is nearby
Close his eyes while he blows the dust off
questions.why: Compressed air drives dust and metal into eyes and skin, and air forced into a cut is very dangerous. Clothes are brushed or vacuumed, and the air line is never pointed at a person.

questions.q: Before clearing the swarf near the guillotine blade, how does Davian make sure nobody can start the machine?
o: Ask another trainee to stand by the start button
Switch it off at the start button only
Hang a note on the guillotine saying he is cleaning it
Isolate it and lock it off with his own lock and a tag
questions.why: Only isolation, locked with his own lock and tagged, makes sure the machine cannot be started while his hands are near the blade. A switch, a note or a helper can all be overridden by mistake.

questions.q: What should be done about the two failed tubes over the marking-out bench?
o: Report them, arrange temporary light, keep old tubes whole
Leave them until enough tubes have failed to change them all
Break the old tubes into the general bin to save space
Move the marking-out work to the dark end of the shop
questions.why: Poor light causes mistakes and hides hazards, so failed lights are reported at once and temporary lighting is used meanwhile. Fluorescent tubes contain mercury, so they are kept whole and sent to an approved collector.

questions.q: Which check of the fume extractor belongs on Davian's weekly list?
o: Take the filters out so that the unit can pull harder
Wash the filters in the sink with a strong degreaser
Empty the spark trap and check the filters
Run it with the hood turned up towards the ceiling
questions.why: A full spark trap and clogged filters cut the airflow, so less fume is captured, and sparks reaching a dirty filter can start a fire. Filters are cleaned or changed only as the maker's manual says, with the unit off.

questions.q: During a 5S Sort, a welder puts a red tag on a heavy jig that nobody recognises. What should happen to it?
o: It goes straight into the scrap skip, as no one claimed it
It stays where it is until somebody trips over it
It goes to the holding area until the supervisor decides
The welder who tagged it takes it home for his own use
questions.why: Red-tagged items wait in a marked holding area for a set time. The supervisor then decides whether to keep the item and give it a place, move it, sell it or dispose of it properly. It might belong to a client or another job.

questions.q: A new degreaser has leaked in the store. Which part of its safety data sheet tells you how to deal with the spill?
o: Section 6, accidental release measures
Section 2, hazard identification
Section 13, disposal considerations
Section 9, physical and chemical properties
questions.why: Section 6 of a safety data sheet gives the PPE, containment and clean-up steps for a spill. Section 2 lists the hazards and section 13 covers disposal of the waste afterwards.
